tracks.title: The if-statement you forgot to write
tracks.text: Lesson 02 point 1 — the dock. A sub-lesson, under the Nexus. The parent lesson made a one-sentence promise… grants, not inheritance. No ambient file system. No ambient network. This lesson is that sentence's machinery. Start with the if-statement you forgot to write. Every permission system you have ever met enforces itself the same way. Code asks… a runtime check answers. A guard clause before the dangerous call. And the whole security story rests on a hope — that every dangerous path has its check, and that nobody added a new one and forgot. [sighs] Audits exist because that hope is routinely wrong. Then agents arrived and made the stakes personal. An agent does not run a fixed set of calls you reviewed. It writes its own calls, at runtime, steered in part by whatever text reaches it. Prompt injection means the workload itself is the adversary you plan for. In that world, one forgotten guard clause is not a bug report. It is an exfiltration. [curious] So here is the question this lesson answers. What if the unauthorized call did not get refused… what if it had no address at all?

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. The Dock is the typed capability membrane between a docked workbook and its Nexus. The host hands the guest exactly the functions its grants permit. An ungranted power is not refused… it does not exist. The word carries two senses, and the parent page already used the first one. The Nexus lesson draws the docking diagram — file in, living software out. The moment a workbook plugs into an engine. This lesson is about what that moment installs. After docking, everything the workbook ever does to the world — every file read, every byte of network, every command, every secret — crosses this one surface. So… the dock is the moment. The Dock is the membrane the docked thing lives against, forever after. Concretely, it is a typed interface — a WIT world called workbooks engine. It declares a handful of imports… session info, vfs query, run command, browse fetch, run command many… and exactly one export — run. The workbook exports its entrypoint. The host decides which imports exist. [curious] That asymmetry is the entire design.

tracks.title: Gated by construction
tracks.text: Now the core mechanism — gated by construction. Here is the whole gate, and it is shorter than most permission middleware's config file. When an Instance starts, the host folds the policy's capability list into an imports map. The base map holds exactly one entry — session info. Always granted… read-only identifiers, nothing more. Then each granted cap merges exactly one more function. The vfs cap adds vfs query. The commands cap adds run command. The browse cap adds browse fetch. A cap that is not in the list adds nothing. And an unknown cap is dropped on the floor. Then wasmtime links the component against that map — and linking is where enforcement happens. Picture the flow. The policy says minimal… its caps fold into a map holding session info, vfs query, run command… and browse fetch is absent. The component arrives at the linker. If the map satisfies its imports, it instantiates and runs. If it hard-imports browse fetch… it fails to link. Before a single guest instruction runs. [excited] There is no code path to forget to guard, because the unauthorized call has no address to jump to. And this is not an aspiration — it is a passing test in the suite. The test loads a component that hard-imports browse fetch, starts it under the minimal profile, and asserts that it errors. The comment in the test says it plainly… minimal does not grant browse, so the host omits the import, and the component fails to link. Enforcement by construction. Its twin test runs a different component under the same minimal profile — one that imports run command, which minimal does grant — and gets back, ok, hello world. [chuckles] Same profile. Two components. Opposite fates… both decided before any guest code executed.

tracks.title: The grant vocabulary
tracks.text: Next — the grant vocabulary. What can a grant actually say? Capabilities come in named bundles, called profiles, and each profile is three numbers and a list. There are four, and these are the real values from the policy module. First, compute… sixty-four megabytes of memory, five seconds per call, and one single cap — vfs. Pure computation plus an ephemeral disk. The true sandbox. Second, minimal… same memory, same clock, but the local caps — commands, exec, durable storage, secrets, queues, and the brokered raw sockets. Third, network… a hundred and twenty-eight megabytes, thirty seconds, and it adds net, llm, and browse. And fourth, posix… two hundred fifty-six megabytes, sixty seconds, the full surface including parallel. The memory number is a hard ceiling — a component growing past it traps. The wall-clock number caps each boundary call… an overrun comes back as a cpu timeout error, and the engine stays responsive. And a profile name nobody recognizes — a typo, a stale config — fails closed, to compute. The least privileged row… never the most. One honest gloss on the names. Minimal means minimal network, not minimal everything — it still grants signing and storage and sockets. If you want the true sandbox, you want compute. And one switch in that table does more work than it looks like. Whether a profile may use high-level HTTP is derived from its caps — true only if net or browse is granted. And that single flag gates the wasi http linkage, the inherited socket pool, and DNS lookup… together. [curious] A non-network profile does not get a filtered network. It reaches no host network stack at all.

tracks.title: Anatomy of one call
tracks.text: A depth rung now — anatomy of one call. Skippable… but this is what a granted import physically does. The wire convention is deliberately primitive. Signatures are integers only. The guest writes its request into its own linear memory and passes a pointer and a length. The host reads those bytes out… does the privileged thing in the engine… writes the reply back into guest memory… and returns the byte count. Or minus one, on denial or error. The guest never holds a socket, a file handle, or a key. It holds bytes it wrote, and bytes it was handed. Even the clock crosses this way — wasm has no wall clock, so host now is a real capability, not a convenience. Walk one brokered TCP request through, end to end. The guest writes host, port, and payload into its own memory, and calls the import with a pointer and a length. The host reads the bytes out. The broker runs its checks… is this principal revoked? Is it rate limited? Then it resolves the hostname once — and if the address is internal, denied, right there. Otherwise it pins the IP. The connection goes to the pinned address — one shot — never to the name. The response comes back, capped at one megabyte… and the host writes it into guest memory. Or returns minus one. That resolve-then-pin step is the detail that closes the DNS rebind window. A second, malicious resolution never gets consulted. And note what the Instance does not have… standard input and output are cut entirely. The typed Dock is the real surface — not a side door next to one.

tracks.title: The broker fleet
tracks.text: Section six — the broker fleet. Every import that exists is half a function. The other half lives in the engine… a broker that holds the dangerous resource, and applies the same cadence on every call. Revocation check… rate check… scope check… size cap… audit. There are nine of them — exec, tcp, udp, tls, secrets, durable storage, queues, parallel, and http — and each one carries named limits straight from the source. Three are worth hearing in full. First, the exec broker. What it executes are registered, sandboxed wasm commands — the same ones toolkits ship. There is no operating-system exec to reach. Its argv is structural — a list handed straight to the command, never a shell string. Its own documentation puts it best… semicolon, rm dash rf slash… is just a literal argument. Never interpreted. [chuckles] Plus a nesting depth of eight, and an eight-megabyte output cap. Second, the http broker — and this row carries a named scar. The guard exists because a mediated fetch with no destination check would have happily fetched the cloud metadata address — one six nine dot two five four dot one six nine dot two five four — and handed the guest its cloud credentials. Now every resolved address is checked against the full internal-range catalog before any socket opens… on the first request, and on every redirect hop after it, five hops at most. Third, the storage broker — and it hides the quietest rule in the lesson. The tenant namespace is captured from the Dock itself. There is no parameter through which a guest names a tenant. A guest can only ever touch its own persistent corner — not because a check said so… but because the question cannot be asked.

tracks.title: Sign, never read
tracks.text: One broker is the emblem of the whole design — sign, never read. The secrets broker holds named credentials per tenant. A Stripe webhook secret… an API key… a JWT signing key. And the guest gets exactly one operation against them. Sign. Picture the round trip. The guest hands over the secret's name — stripe underscore webhook — plus a payload. The host calls the broker. Inside the engine, the broker computes an HMAC, SHA two fifty-six, with the named key. And thirty-two bytes of signature come back. The key never crossed. The broker's own documentation states the invariant flatly… there is deliberately no function that returns a secret's value. Now walk the consequence through. A workbook can verify and sign Stripe webhooks forever — real authentication, production grade. And then assume the worst case the agents lesson warns about. The guest is fully compromised… a prompt-injected agent, actively trying to exfiltrate. [curious] What can it steal? Signatures… of data it already had. The credential is not in its address space. Not in its imports. Not anywhere it can name. The parent page claimed that secrets stay in the engine. That is not a policy the engine enforces. [excited] It is a function the engine never built.

tracks.title: Two kinds of gate
tracks.text: Another depth rung — two kinds of gate. One membrane… three guest shapes… and they do not all gate the same way, which is worth being honest about. First — components, and compiled Rust core modules. These gate by presence. The host omits the import, and a guest that needs it fails at link. A component fails at start. A Rust module fails at the call that forces instantiation. Second — the JavaScript lane. It cannot gate by presence, because QuickJS commands share one fixed harness that imports every host function unconditionally. So it gates by behavior. The function exists… and refuses. A denied call returns minus one, which surfaces to the script as a null. The verdict, in one sentence. Presence-gating fails early and loudly… behavior-gating fails late and quietly. Both end at the same place — the privileged operation runs in the engine or not at all, and zero native code executes either way. But only the first two make the denial a structural fact. The third is a runtime check… the very thing this lesson opened by distrusting… confined to the one lane whose fixed wiring leaves no alternative.

tracks.title: The paper trail
tracks.text: Section nine — the paper trail. A membrane you cannot watch is a membrane you cannot operate. Every crossing leaves a record, in three layers. First… steps. Every run-command invocation appends one line to the Instance's step log — tool name, exit code, duration, timestamp — in exactly the shape agent tool calls are logged, counted by the same summary code. A workbook calling a command through the Dock, and an agent calling a tool, are the same event to the telemetry layer. Second… denials. Every broker outcome bumps an atomic counter, keyed by broker, outcome, and reason. So the question after an incident is a read. Three denials on the net broker, all for SSRF, against twelve allows — that pattern means a guest is probing internal targets. Denials also land in a forensics ring… the last one hundred twenty-eight, newest first, each with the target the guest tried to reach. And that target string is guest controlled — so it is truncated to five hundred twelve bytes before storage. [chuckles] An attacker should not get to fill host memory with the evidence against them. Every outcome also emits a standard telemetry event, so Prometheus or a SIEM can watch the membrane without touching its internals. And third… revocation. The brokers consult a revocation set on every privileged call. Which means cutting off a principal takes effect on the very next call — mid flight, no teardown. Revoke a tenant, and its next sign call returns minus one… with the denial in the ring, reason attached. Under all of it sits a per-tenant rate floor — a hundred and twenty thousand broker calls per sixty-second window, about two thousand per second. Not a meter on legitimate throughput… a tripwire for a guest spinning in a tight loop.

tracks.title: Where the membrane ends
tracks.text: Now the honest part — where the membrane ends. Six edges, stated plainly. First… the JavaScript lane is a runtime check. The harness imports everything, so a JS guest only discovers a denial at call time, as a null. The by-construction story is true for components and Rust modules — for JS, it is behavior-gating wearing the same brokers. Second… the CPU cap is a wall-clock trap, not an interrupt. An overrunning call returns a timeout error and the engine stays responsive — but the runaway worker thread itself is not yet reclaimed. Epoch-based interruption is open work… tracked, and unfinished. The caller is protected today. The thread is freed tomorrow. Third… presence-gating can fail late. A component fails at start — the best possible time. A lazily instantiated module fails at the first call that forces instantiation… later than you would like to learn about a missing grant. Fourth… minus one tells the guest nothing. Deny and error look identical from inside — deliberately, since a probe should not get a capability map for free. The cost is that you debug from the host side, via the audit ring. Fifth… the Dock governs crossings, not residence. Pure-compute mischief that never touches an import — burning its memory ceiling, spinning until the timeout — is the wasm sandbox's story, not the membrane's. The membrane only ever sees what tries to leave. And sixth… the typed surface is stringly. Most imports speak JSON in strings. A small guest-side SDK papers over that with typed, fallible wrappers — each cap behind a feature flag, so only granted caps are even linked. Honest reading… the membrane's safety is structural. Its ergonomics are a library.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Why did my component fail to instantiate? Almost always — it imports a capability its profile does not grant, and the system is working. Match the component's imports to the profile's cap list. The error arrived before any of your code ran… which is the design doing you a favor. The same mismatch discovered in production would be a security finding. Can a guest detect which caps it has? Not by enumeration — there is no import that lists imports. A component knows implicitly, because it linked. A JS guest finds out empirically… call, and check for null. Does a granted net cap mean open internet? No. The SSRF floor applies to every host-mediated fetch regardless of grants, on the first request and on each re-checked redirect hop. Net opens the door to the public internet… not to your engine's neighborhood. A secret-holding tenant goes rogue — now what? Revoke the principal. The very next call returns minus one, mid flight, no teardown. And the worst case was already bounded — the tenant only ever held signatures… never the key. Last one. Is minus one an error, or a denial? [chuckles] Yes. The guest cannot tell, on purpose. The host can — the audit ring holds the last hundred and twenty-eight denials, with broker, reason, target, and timestamp. When in doubt… check the ring, not the guest's logs.

tracks.title: Back up to the engine
tracks.text: So that is the Dock. A permission is not a rule checked at call time — it is a function that exists, or does not. The host builds the import table from the grants… an ungranted capability has no address… and every import that does exist is half a function, with a broker holding the dangerous half inside the engine. The emblem is the secret that signs but can never be read. [curious] If you came down from the parent lesson, the way back up is short — the Nexus, lesson two, owns the engine this membrane belongs to. And three siblings take the deeper slices… capabilities, for the profiles cap by cap. Secrets, for the full sign-never-read lifecycle. And networking, for the brokered sockets and the SSRF guard. The membrane is one idea, told once… everything else is what crosses it.
